concepts.def: Each planet moves in an elliptical orbit with the Sun at one focus of the ellipse (not at its centre). A circle is the special case of an ellipse in which the two foci coincide; in IB calculations orbits are taken as circular.

The line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal times. In an elliptical orbit the planet therefore moves fastest when nearest the Sun and slowest when furthest from it. In a circular orbit the law means the speed is constant.

The square of the time period T of a planet's orbit is proportional to the cube of its mean distance from the Sun: T² ∝ r³, so T²/r³ is the same for every planet of the Sun. For a circular orbit, equating GMm/r² to mv²/r with v = 2πr/T gives T²/r³ = 4π²/GM, so the constant depends on the central mass M: moons of Jupiter share one value, planets of the Sun another.
The time T taken for one complete orbit. For a circular orbit of radius r at speed v, T = 2πr/v. SI unit: second (s), although days or years are often quoted.

Every point mass attracts every other point mass with a force along the line joining them, proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation: F = Gm₁m₂/r². The two bodies exert equal and opposite forces on each other (a Newton's third law pair), whatever their masses.

The constant in Newton's law of gravitation, G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². It is the same everywhere, which is why the law is called universal. Its small value is why gravitational forces between everyday objects are tiny.

An idealised body whose whole mass is located at a single point, so that its size and shape play no part. 'Point' refers to size, not to how much mass the body has: the Sun can be modelled as a point mass.

concepts.term: Uniform sphere treated as a point mass
concepts.def: At any point outside a sphere of uniform density (or any spherically symmetric body), the gravitational field is exactly the same as if the whole mass were concentrated at the centre. This holds however close to the surface the point is, so r in F = Gm₁m₂/r² is measured centre to centre. Any extended body can also be treated as a point mass when the separation is very large compared with its size.

The gravitational force per unit mass experienced by a small point mass placed at a point: g = F/m. It is a vector, directed towards the mass producing the field. SI unit: N kg⁻¹, which is equivalent to m s⁻², because g is also the acceleration of free fall at that point. A small test mass is specified so that it does not disturb the field it is measuring.

concepts.term: Field strength of a point or spherical mass
concepts.def: At distance r from the centre of a point mass or uniform sphere of mass M, g = GM/r². The field is radial and follows an inverse-square law: doubling r reduces g to one quarter. It depends on M and r, not on the mass of the object placed in the field.

Around a point or spherical mass the field is radial: directed towards the centre with a magnitude that falls with distance. Close to the surface of a planet, over a region small compared with its radius, the field is assumed uniform: the same magnitude and direction everywhere.

concepts.term: Resultant field on the line joining two bodies
concepts.def: Between two bodies the two fields point in opposite directions along the line joining them, so the resultant is the difference of their magnitudes. It is zero where GM₁/x² = GM₂/(d − x)², a point nearer the less massive body.

Lines showing the direction of the gravitational force on a small mass at each point. For a gravitational field they point towards the mass producing the field; they never cross; and their spacing shows the field strength (closer lines, stronger field). Around an isolated uniform sphere they are radial and point inwards; in a uniform field they are parallel and equally spaced. Field lines are not the paths that moving masses follow.

concepts.term: Gravitational potential energy E_p of a system
concepts.def: The work done to assemble the system from infinite separation of its components. Because the components attract, bringing them together from infinity requires negative work from an external agent, so E_p is negative and becomes less negative (increases) as the components move apart. It is a property of the system, not of one body. SI unit: joule (J).

E_p = −Gm₁m₂/r, where r is the separation of the centres of mass of the two bodies. E_p = 0 at infinite separation and is negative at any finite separation. The change on moving from r₁ to r₂ is ΔE_p = Gm₁m₂(1/r₁ − 1/r₂), positive when the separation increases. Near a surface, over small heights, this reduces to ΔE_p ≈ mgΔh.

The work done per unit mass in bringing a small mass from infinity to a point: V_g = −GM/r for a point or spherical mass M. It is a scalar, zero at infinity and negative everywhere else, rising towards zero with distance. SI unit: J kg⁻¹. The gravitational potential energy of a mass m at that point is mV_g.

The rate of change of gravitational potential with distance, ΔV_g/Δr. The field strength is minus the potential gradient: g = −ΔV_g/Δr. The minus sign means the field points in the direction in which the potential decreases, towards the mass. On a graph of V_g against r, the magnitude of g is the gradient of the curve.

concepts.term: Work done moving a mass in a gravitational field
concepts.def: The work done by an external force in moving a mass m between two points, with no change in kinetic energy, is W = mΔV_g, where ΔV_g = V_final − V_initial. It is positive when the mass moves to a higher (less negative) potential and does not depend on the path taken.

A surface on which every point has the same gravitational potential. Around an isolated uniform sphere the equipotentials are concentric spheres; in a uniform field they are parallel planes. Drawn at equal intervals of potential, they are closer together where the field is stronger, so around a planet they get further apart with distance.

Gravitational field lines cross equipotential surfaces at right angles. No work is done in moving a mass along an equipotential, because the gravitational force has no component along it; the field is not zero there, it is perpendicular to the surface.

The minimum speed a body must have at a point to reach infinite separation from a mass M with no further energy input: ½mv_esc² − GMm/r = 0, so v_esc = √(2GM/r). It depends on the distance r from the centre and not on the mass of the escaping body; it is lower at greater distances. SI unit: m s⁻¹.

The speed of a body in a circular orbit of radius r around a large mass M. The gravitational force provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v_orbital = √(GM/r). It is independent of the orbiting body's mass and decreases as r increases. At any r, v_esc = √2 × v_orbital.

concepts.term: Energy of a satellite in a circular orbit
concepts.def: For a satellite of mass m in a circular orbit of radius r: E_k = GMm/2r, E_p = −GMm/r and total energy E = −GMm/2r = −E_k. A larger orbit has less kinetic energy but more (less negative) potential energy and more total energy. To escape from the orbit, the total energy must be raised to zero.

concepts.term: Orbital decay due to atmospheric drag
concepts.def: A small viscous drag force from the thin upper atmosphere removes energy from a satellite, so its total energy −GMm/2r becomes more negative and its orbital radius decreases. Because v_orbital = √(GM/r), its speed increases: as it spirals slowly inwards, the loss of E_p is twice the gain in E_k, the other half being dissipated by the drag.

mcqs.q: Kepler's third law describes the orbits of the planets around the Sun. Taking each orbit as a circle of radius r with time period T, which statement expresses the law?
options: T/r has the same value for every planet that orbits the Sun.
T has the same value for every planet, whatever its distance.
T²/r³ has the same value for every planet that orbits the Sun.
T²/r³ has one value for all orbiting bodies, whatever they orbit.
mcqs.specStatementText: Kepler’s three laws of orbital motion
mcqs.explain: This is Kepler's third law, T² ∝ r³. For circular orbits it follows from GMm/r² = m(2π/T)²r, which gives T²/r³ = 4π²/GM, the same for every planet because M is the Sun's mass.
rationales: A student who thinks all planets move at the same speed would expect T to be proportional to r and picks this. Outer planets are also slower: from T² ∝ r³ and v = 2πr/T, v ∝ 1/√r, so T grows as r^(3/2): it is T²/r³, not T/r, that is constant.

A student who pictures the planets turning together like points on a wheel picks this. The planets are not linked; each has the period set by gravity at its own distance, from 88 days for Mercury to 165 years for Neptune.
This is Kepler's third law, T² ∝ r³. For circular orbits it follows from GMm/r² = m(2π/T)²r, which gives T²/r³ = 4π²/GM, the same for every planet because M is the Sun's mass.
A student who treats the constant as universal picks this. T²/r³ = 4π²/GM contains the mass M of the central body, so the moons of Jupiter share a different value from the planets of the Sun.

mcqs.q: A comet moves around the Sun in a highly elliptical orbit. Which statement about the comet agrees with Kepler's laws?
options: It moves at the same speed at every point of its orbit.
It moves fastest when it is furthest from the Sun.
The Sun is at the centre of its elliptical orbit.
It moves fastest when it is nearest the Sun.
mcqs.specStatementText: Kepler’s three laws of orbital motion
mcqs.explain: Kepler's second law: the line from the Sun to the comet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Near the Sun the swept triangle is short, so the comet must cover a longer arc in the same time: it is fastest at its closest approach and slowest at its furthest point.
rationales: A student who reads 'equal areas in equal times' as 'equal distances in equal times' picks this. The area swept out depends on the comet's distance from the Sun as well as its speed, so near the Sun, where the swept triangle is short, the comet must move faster to sweep the same area.

A student who pictures the orbit like a turning wheel, sweeping equal angles in equal times, expects the comet to move fastest where it is furthest out and picks this. Kepler's second law is about equal AREAS: far from the Sun a long, thin triangle has a short arc, so the comet is slowest there.

A student who places the Sun at the centre, as in most drawings of near-circular orbits, picks this. Kepler's first law puts the Sun at one focus of the ellipse, off-centre; that is why the comet's distance from the Sun varies so much around its orbit.

Kepler's second law: the line from the Sun to the comet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Near the Sun the swept triangle is short, so the comet must cover a longer arc in the same time: it is fastest at its closest approach and slowest at its furthest point.

mcqs.q: Io and Europa are moons of Jupiter, and their orbits may be taken as circular. Io has an orbital radius of 4.22 × 10⁸ m and a time period of 1.77 days. Europa has an orbital radius of 6.71 × 10⁸ m. What is the time period of Europa?
options: 2.81 days
3.55 days
1.77 days
4.48 days
mcqs.specStatementText: Kepler’s three laws of orbital motion
mcqs.explain: By Kepler's third law T² ∝ r³ for moons of the same planet, so T_E = T_I × (r_E/r_I)^(3/2) = 1.77 × (6.71/4.22)^(3/2) = 1.77 × 2.005 = 3.55 days.
mcqs.working: Kepler's third law for two moons of the same planet: T_E²/r_E³ = T_I²/r_I³ ⇒ T_E = T_I (r_E/r_I)^(3/2). r_E/r_I = 6.71 × 10⁸ m / 4.22 × 10⁸ m = 1.590; 1.590^(3/2) = 2.005. T_E = 1.77 days × 2.005 = 3.55 days.
rationales: A student who assumes the moons move at the same speed takes T ∝ r: 1.77 × 6.71/4.22 = 2.81 days. Europa is further out and also slower, so its period grows faster than its radius.
By Kepler's third law T² ∝ r³ for moons of the same planet, so T_E = T_I × (r_E/r_I)^(3/2) = 1.77 × (6.71/4.22)^(3/2) = 1.77 × 2.005 = 3.55 days.
A student who thinks orbiting bodies share one period, like points on a rotating wheel, gives Io's period again. Each moon's period is set by its own radius: T² ∝ r³.
A student who uses T ∝ r², by analogy with the inverse-square law, gets 1.77 × (6.71/4.22)² = 4.48 days. The law is T² ∝ r³, so the radius ratio is raised to the power 3/2, not 2.

mcqs.q: The Earth exerts a gravitational force of 2.0 × 10²⁰ N on the Moon. The mass of the Moon is about 1.2% of the mass of the Earth. Which statement about the gravitational force that the Moon exerts on the Earth is correct?
options: It is 2.0 × 10²⁰ N, and it pulls the Earth towards the Moon.
It is about 1.2% of 2.0 × 10²⁰ N, as the Moon has far less mass.
It is zero, as a small body cannot attract a much larger one.
It is zero, as the Moon has no air and so has no gravity.
mcqs.specStatementText: Newton’s universal law of gravitation as given by F = G m₁m₂/r² for bodies treated as point masses
mcqs.explain: The two forces are a Newton's third law pair: equal in size, opposite in direction. F = Gm₁m₂/r² contains the product of both masses, so the same value applies to each body. The force on the Earth points towards the Moon.
mcqs.working: Newton's third law: F(Moon on Earth) = F(Earth on Moon) = 2.0 × 10²⁰ N, opposite in direction. F = Gm₁m₂/r² is symmetric in m₁ and m₂, so the mass ratio (1.2%) does not enter.
rationales: The two forces are a Newton's third law pair: equal in size, opposite in direction. F = Gm₁m₂/r² contains the product of both masses, so the same value applies to each body. The force on the Earth points towards the Moon.

A student who thinks the more massive body pulls harder scales the force by the mass ratio. The forces are equal; the Moon's small mass means the same force gives it a large acceleration, while the Earth's acceleration is about 81 times smaller.
A student who thinks only big bodies have gravity picks this. Every mass attracts every other mass, and the Moon's pull on the Earth is strong enough to raise the ocean tides.

A student who thinks gravity needs an atmosphere picks this. Gravity depends only on mass and distance and acts across a vacuum: the Moon has no atmosphere, yet astronauts on it had weight, and it pulls on the Earth.

mcqs.q: A satellite of mass 1200 kg orbits the Earth at a height of 600 km above the surface. The Earth has mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6370 km. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². What is the gravitational force that the Earth exerts on the satellite?
mcqs.specStatementText: Newton’s universal law of gravitation as given by F = G m₁m₂/r² for bodies treated as point masses
mcqs.explain: r is measured from the Earth's centre: r = 6370 km + 600 km = 6970 km = 6.97 × 10⁶ m. F = GMm/r² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴ × 1200 / (6.97 × 10⁶)² = 9.84 × 10³ N.
rationales: A student who uses the height, 6.0 × 10⁵ m, as r gets 1.33 × 10⁶ N. The Earth acts as a point mass at its centre, so r = R + h = 6.97 × 10⁶ m.
A student who correctly adds 6370 km + 600 km but substitutes r = 6970 without converting to metres gets an answer 10⁶ times too large. G is in N m² kg⁻², so r must be in metres: 6.97 × 10⁶ m.
r is measured from the Earth's centre: r = 6370 km + 600 km = 6970 km = 6.97 × 10⁶ m. F = GMm/r² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴ × 1200 / (6.97 × 10⁶)² = 9.84 × 10³ N.
A student who uses the Earth's radius as r finds the force at the surface, 1.18 × 10⁴ N. The satellite is 600 km higher, so r = 6.97 × 10⁶ m and the force is about 16% smaller.

mcqs.q: A planet is a sphere of uniform density. Why can it be treated as a point mass at its centre when calculating the gravitational force on a satellite orbiting it?
options: A satellite is usually far away compared with the planet's radius, so the planet looks like a point.
The satellite's mass is tiny compared with the planet's, so the planet's size is irrelevant.
All of the planet's mass is concentrated at its centre, where its gravity comes from.
At any point outside a uniform sphere, its field is that of a point mass at its centre.
mcqs.specStatementText: conditions under which extended bodies can be treated as point masses
mcqs.explain: This is the condition in the guide: at any point outside a sphere of uniform density, however close to its surface, the combined attraction of all its parts equals that of a point mass at the centre. So r in F = GMm/r² is measured from the planet's centre.
rationales: A student who thinks the point-mass model is only an approximation for distant bodies picks this. For a uniform sphere the result is exact at every point outside it, however close: a satellite in low orbit is only a little more than one planet radius from the centre, yet the model applies exactly.

A student who hears 'point mass' as 'small mass' picks this. The point-mass model depends on the shape and density of the planet, not on the mass ratio; a very massive uniform star is also treated as a point mass.

A student who takes 'as if concentrated at the centre' literally picks this. The mass is spread through the whole planet and every part attracts the satellite; only the combined effect equals that of a point mass at the centre.

This is the condition in the guide: at any point outside a sphere of uniform density, however close to its surface, the combined attraction of all its parts equals that of a point mass at the centre. So r in F = GMm/r² is measured from the planet's centre.

mcqs.q: Which statement defines the gravitational field strength g at a point?
options: The gravitational force acting on any object placed at that point, in newtons.
The gravitational force per unit mass on a small point mass placed at that point.
The acceleration of free fall at that point, which is 9.8 m s⁻² at every point.
The force per unit mass on a small point mass, directed away from the mass producing the field.
mcqs.specStatementText: that gravitational field strength g at a point is the force per unit mass experienced by a small point mass at that point as given by g = F/m = GM/r²
mcqs.explain: This is the definition in the guide: g = F/m for a small test mass, one small enough not to disturb the field. The unit is N kg⁻¹, equivalent to m s⁻².
mcqs.working: Definition: g = F/m, the force per unit mass on a small test mass; unit N kg⁻¹ (= m s⁻²). The value 9.8 m s⁻² applies only at the Earth's surface.
rationales: A student who confuses field strength with weight picks this. The force depends on the object's mass; the field strength is the force PER KILOGRAM, so it is the same for every object at that point.
This is the definition in the guide: g = F/m for a small test mass, one small enough not to disturb the field. The unit is N kg⁻¹, equivalent to m s⁻².
A student who treats g as a universal constant picks this. 9.8 m s⁻² is the value at the Earth's surface; g = GM/r², so it is smaller at height and different on other planets.

A student who carries over the outward direction of electric field lines from a positive charge picks this. Gravity always attracts, so the force on a small mass, and therefore the field, points towards the mass producing the field.

mcqs.q: At the surface of the Earth, g = 9.8 N kg⁻¹. Planet X has the same mass as the Earth but half its radius. Both may be treated as uniform spheres. What is the gravitational field strength at the surface of planet X?
options: 39.2 N kg⁻¹
19.6 N kg⁻¹
9.80 N kg⁻¹
4.90 N kg⁻¹
mcqs.specStatementText: that gravitational field strength g at a point is the force per unit mass experienced by a small point mass at that point as given by g = F/m = GM/r²
mcqs.explain: g = GM/R². With the same M and half the R, g increases by a factor 1/(0.5)² = 4: 4 × 9.8 = 39.2 N kg⁻¹.
mcqs.working: g = GM/R². g_X/g_E = (M_X/M_E)(R_E/R_X)² = 1 × 2² = 4. g_X = 4 × 9.8 N kg⁻¹ = 39.2 N kg⁻¹.
rationales: g = GM/R². With the same M and half the R, g increases by a factor 1/(0.5)² = 4: 4 × 9.8 = 39.2 N kg⁻¹.
A student who treats g as inversely proportional to R (forgetting the square) doubles the value. g = GM/R², so halving R multiplies g by four.
A student who assumes g has the same value everywhere gives the Earth's value. g = GM/R² depends on the planet's radius as well as its mass.
A student who thinks a smaller planet must have weaker gravity halves the value. Planet X has the same mass, but its surface is closer to its centre, so the field there is stronger.

mcqs.q: The Earth (mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg) and the Moon (mass 7.35 × 10²² kg) are 3.84 × 10⁸ m apart, centre to centre. At one point on the line joining their centres, the resultant gravitational field strength is zero. How far is this point from the centre of the Earth?
mcqs.specStatementText: that gravitational field strength g at a point is the force per unit mass experienced by a small point mass at that point as given by g = F/m = GM/r²
mcqs.explain: Set GM_E/x² = GM_M/(d − x)²: x/(d − x) = √(M_E/M_M) = √81.2 = 9.01, so x = 9.01d/10.01 = 3.46 × 10⁸ m, about 90% of the way to the Moon.
mcqs.working: Fields are antiparallel on the line joining the centres, so the resultant is zero where GM_E/x² = GM_M/(d − x)². √(M_E/M_M) = √(5.97 × 10²⁴ / 7.35 × 10²²) = √81.2 = 9.01. x = 9.01(d − x) ⇒ x = 9.01 × 3.84 × 10⁸ m / 10.01 = 3.46 × 10⁸ m from the Earth's centre.
rationales: A student who forgets that the fields fall as 1/r² sets M_E/x = M_M/(d − x) and gets x = d × 81.2/82.2 = 3.79 × 10⁸ m. The inverse-square law puts the square root of the mass ratio into the answer.
Set GM_E/x² = GM_M/(d − x)²: x/(d − x) = √(M_E/M_M) = √81.2 = 9.01, so x = 9.01d/10.01 = 3.46 × 10⁸ m, about 90% of the way to the Moon.
A student who assumes the fields cancel halfway picks the midpoint. The Earth is 81 times more massive, so its field is much stronger at the midpoint; the zero point is much closer to the Moon.

A student who confuses the zero-field point with the centre of mass gets x = d × M_M/(M_E + M_M) = 4.67 × 10⁶ m, which is inside the Earth. The centre of mass balances masses × distances; the zero-field point balances masses ÷ distances².

mcqs.q: A student sketches the gravitational field lines around an isolated planet that is a uniform sphere. Which description of a correct sketch is right?
options: Straight radial lines pointing inwards to the planet's centre, closer together near its surface.
Straight radial lines pointing outwards from the planet's centre, closer together near it.
Parallel lines all pointing 'down' in one direction, equally spaced at all distances.
Curved lines that leave the planet near one pole and re-enter it near the other.
mcqs.specStatementText: gravitational field lines.
mcqs.explain: The force on a small mass points towards the centre of the planet, so the lines are radial and point inwards. They converge on the planet, so they are closest together near the surface, where the field is strongest.
rationales: The force on a small mass points towards the centre of the planet, so the lines are radial and point inwards. They converge on the planet, so they are closest together near the surface, where the field is strongest.
A student who borrows the pattern for a positive charge picks this. Gravity always attracts, so the arrows on gravitational field lines point towards the mass, not away from it.

A student who pictures gravity as a single fixed 'down' picks this. 'Down' is towards the centre of the planet, so around a whole planet the lines are radial. Parallel, equally spaced lines apply only to a small region near the surface.

A student who links gravity with magnetism draws the Earth's magnetic field pattern. Gravitational field lines around a sphere are straight and radial; they never form loops, and gravity acts on all matter, magnetic or not.

mcqs.q: Close to the surface of a planet, over a region a few kilometres across, the gravitational field is drawn as parallel, equally spaced field lines pointing vertically downwards. What does this pattern show about the field in that region?
options: Any object released or thrown in the region moves along one of the field lines.
The field acts only along the lines drawn, with no field in the gaps between them.
The field strength has the same size and direction at every point in the region.
A heavier object placed in the region experiences a larger field strength.
mcqs.specStatementText: gravitational field lines.
mcqs.explain: Parallel lines show the same direction everywhere, and equal spacing shows the same strength everywhere: a uniform field. This is the assumed uniform field close to the surface of a planet.
rationales: A student who reads field lines as paths picks this. The lines show the direction of the force, not of the motion. A ball thrown sideways follows a parabola across the lines; only an object released from rest falls along one.
A student who takes the lines literally picks this. The lines are a sample; the field exists at every point, including between the lines, and more lines could be drawn anywhere.
Parallel lines show the same direction everywhere, and equal spacing shows the same strength everywhere: a uniform field. This is the assumed uniform field close to the surface of a planet.
A student who confuses field strength with force picks this. A heavier object feels a larger FORCE, mg, but the field strength g, the force per kilogram, is the same for every object at a point.

mcqs.q: The gravitational potential energy E_p of a system is the work done to assemble the system from infinite separation of its components. Why is E_p of an Earth–satellite system negative?
options: The minus sign shows that the potential energy is directed towards the centre of the Earth.
Positive work is needed to bring them together, so the minus sign is only a convention.
Energy has been used up in bringing them together, leaving the system with an energy deficit.
The bodies attract, so the work done to bring them together from infinity is negative.
mcqs.specStatementText: that the gravitational potential energy E_p of a system is the work done to assemble the system from infinite separation of the components of the system
mcqs.explain: As the bodies approach, gravity pulls them together; to assemble the system without them speeding up, an external agent must hold them back, so it does negative work. E_p is zero at infinity and negative at any finite separation.
rationales: A student who reads every minus sign as a direction picks this. Energy is a scalar and has no direction; the minus sign says E_p is less than its value at infinite separation, which is zero.

A student who equates assembling with putting energy in picks this. The attraction does the pulling; the agent holds the bodies back and does negative work. The sign follows from the definition, not from an arbitrary choice.

A student who thinks energy is consumed reads the negative value as a debt. No energy is destroyed: the E_p lost as the bodies come together goes into other stores. The value is negative only because zero is set at infinite separation.

As the bodies approach, gravity pulls them together; to assemble the system without them speeding up, an external agent must hold them back, so it does negative work. E_p is zero at infinity and negative at any finite separation.

mcqs.q: A satellite of mass 500 kg is moved from a circular orbit of radius 6.80 × 10⁶ m to a circular orbit of radius 2.04 × 10⁷ m around the Earth, of mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². The gravitational field strength at the Earth's surface is 9.8 N kg⁻¹. What is the change in the gravitational potential energy of the Earth–satellite system?
mcqs.specStatementText: the gravitational potential energy for a two-body system as given by E_p = −G m₁m₂/r where r is the separation between the centre of mass of the two bodies
mcqs.explain: ΔE_p = E_p,final − E_p,initial = −GMm/r₂ − (−GMm/r₁) = GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂) = 1.99 × 10¹⁷ × (1.471 × 10⁻⁷ − 4.90 × 10⁻⁸) = +1.95 × 10¹⁰ J. E_p increases (becomes less negative) as the satellite moves out.
rationales: A student who compares the sizes of GMm/r sees it get smaller and concludes E_p decreases. E_p is negative: it rises from −2.93 × 10¹⁰ J to −9.76 × 10⁹ J, an increase.

A student who uses ΔE_p = mgΔh with g = 9.8 N kg⁻¹ over 1.36 × 10⁷ m gets 6.66 × 10¹⁰ J. g falls as 1/r² over this distance, so mgΔh with the surface value overestimates the change several times over.

ΔE_p = E_p,final − E_p,initial = −GMm/r₂ − (−GMm/r₁) = GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂) = 1.99 × 10¹⁷ × (1.471 × 10⁻⁷ − 4.90 × 10⁻⁸) = +1.95 × 10¹⁰ J. E_p increases (becomes less negative) as the satellite moves out.

A student who takes the potential energy at the starting orbit, E_p = −GMm/r₁, as the change gets −2.93 × 10¹⁰ J. That is the potential energy of the system relative to infinite separation, not the change between the two orbits: ΔE_p = E_p,final − E_p,initial = −9.76 × 10⁹ J − (−2.93 × 10¹⁰ J) = +1.95 × 10¹⁰ J.

mcqs.q: A probe of mass m is lifted from the surface of a planet of radius R to a height R above the surface. The field strength at the surface is g. A student calculates the gain in gravitational potential energy using ΔE_p = mgΔh with Δh = R. How does the student's answer compare with the true gain, found from E_p = −GMm/r?
options: 1.0 times the true gain
4.0 times the true gain
1.6 times the true gain
2.0 times the true gain
mcqs.specStatementText: the gravitational potential energy for a two-body system as given by E_p = −G m₁m₂/r where r is the separation between the centre of mass of the two bodies
mcqs.explain: True gain: GMm(1/R − 1/2R) = GMm/2R. Since g = GM/R², GMm/2R = ½mgR. The student's mgR is therefore 2.0 times the true gain, because g falls as the probe rises and less work is needed for each metre higher up.
mcqs.working: True ΔE_p = GMm(1/R − 1/2R) = GMm/2R. With GM = gR²: ΔE_p = mgR/2. Student: mgΔh = mgR. Ratio = mgR ÷ (mgR/2) = 2.0.
rationales: A student who thinks mgΔh holds at any height expects the two to agree. g at height R is only g/4, so the work done per metre falls as the probe rises and mgR overestimates the gain.

A student who takes the true gain as m(g/4)R, using the field strength at the final height for the whole journey, gets a ratio of 4. The field is stronger (up to g) over the lower part of the path, so the true gain is ½mgR, not ¼mgR.
A student who averages the end values of g, (g + g/4)/2 = 5g/8, gets a ratio of 1.6. That average is valid only if g falls linearly; g ∝ 1/r², so the exact result from E_p = −GMm/r must be used.

True gain: GMm(1/R − 1/2R) = GMm/2R. Since g = GM/R², GMm/2R = ½mgR. The student's mgR is therefore 2.0 times the true gain, because g falls as the probe rises and less work is needed for each metre higher up.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the gravitational potential V_g at a point outside a planet is correct?
options: It is the gravitational potential energy of any mass at the point, measured in joules.
It is the work done per unit mass to bring a small mass from infinity to the point, and is negative.
It is zero at the planet's surface and increases with height above it, as mgh does.
It is the gravitational force per unit mass on a small mass at the point, directed inwards.
mcqs.specStatementText: that the gravitational potential V_g at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a mass from infinity to that point as given by V_g = −GM/r
mcqs.explain: This is the guide's definition, V_g = −GM/r. It is zero at infinity and negative at every finite distance, because the planet attracts the mass as it is brought in. Unit: J kg⁻¹.
rationales: A student who treats potential and potential energy as the same picks this. V_g is energy PER UNIT MASS (J kg⁻¹); the potential energy of a mass m at the point is mV_g, in joules.
This is the guide's definition, V_g = −GM/r. It is zero at infinity and negative at every finite distance, because the planet attracts the mass as it is brought in. Unit: J kg⁻¹.

A student who carries over the ground-level zero from mgh picks this. In this course V_g = 0 at infinity, so at the surface V_g = −GM/R; it does increase with height, but towards zero, never above it.
A student who merges potential and field strength picks this. Force per unit mass is the field strength g (a vector, N kg⁻¹); potential is work per unit mass (a scalar, J kg⁻¹).

mcqs.q: The Moon has mass 7.35 × 10²² kg and radius 1.74 × 10⁶ m. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². What is the gravitational potential due to the Moon at a point 1.00 × 10⁶ m above its surface?
mcqs.specStatementText: that the gravitational potential V_g at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a mass from infinity to that point as given by V_g = −GM/r
rationales: A student who uses the height, 1.00 × 10⁶ m, as r gets −4.90 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. r is measured from the Moon's centre: r = R + h = 2.74 × 10⁶ m.
A student who uses the Moon's radius as r finds the potential at the surface, −2.82 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. The point is 1.00 × 10⁶ m higher, where the potential is less negative.

A student who takes V_g = 0 at the surface finds the potential difference from the surface, +1.03 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. In this course V_g = 0 at infinity, so the potential at any finite distance is negative.

mcqs.q: Two equipotential surfaces around the Earth are 1.00 × 10⁵ m apart along a radial line. The inner surface has V_g = −6.251 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹ and the outer surface has V_g = −6.155 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹. Taking r as increasing outwards from the Earth's centre, what is the average gravitational field strength g between the two surfaces?
options: +9.6 N kg⁻¹ (directed away from the Earth)
−9.8 N kg⁻¹ (directed towards the Earth’s centre)
0 N kg⁻¹ (each surface is an equipotential)
−9.6 N kg⁻¹ (directed towards the Earth)
mcqs.specStatementText: the gravitational field strength g as the gravitational potential gradient as given by g = −ΔV_g/Δr
mcqs.explain: g = −ΔV_g/Δr = −(−6.155 × 10⁷ − (−6.251 × 10⁷))/1.00 × 10⁵ = −(9.6 × 10⁵)/(1.00 × 10⁵) = −9.6 N kg⁻¹. The minus sign means the field points towards decreasing r, towards the Earth.
mcqs.working: ΔV_g = V_outer − V_inner = −6.155 × 10⁷ − (−6.251 × 10⁷) = +9.6 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. Δr = +1.00 × 10⁵ m. g = −ΔV_g/Δr = −9.6 N kg⁻¹, i.e. 9.6 N kg⁻¹ directed towards the Earth.
rationales: A student who drops the minus sign in g = −ΔV_g/Δr gets +9.6 N kg⁻¹. The potential increases outwards, so the field points the other way, towards lower potential and towards the Earth.

A student who takes g as 9.8 N kg⁻¹ everywhere picks this. The inner surface is close to the Earth's surface, where g is about 9.8 N kg⁻¹, but g decreases with height (g = GM/r²), so it is smaller across the gap. The average field between the surfaces must come from the data: g = −ΔV_g/Δr = −(9.6 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹)/(1.00 × 10⁵ m) = −9.6 N kg⁻¹.
A student who thinks there is no field on an equipotential picks this. The potential is constant ALONG each surface but changes BETWEEN them, and it is this change across the gap that gives g.
g = −ΔV_g/Δr = −(−6.155 × 10⁷ − (−6.251 × 10⁷))/1.00 × 10⁵ = −(9.6 × 10⁵)/(1.00 × 10⁵) = −9.6 N kg⁻¹. The minus sign means the field points towards decreasing r, towards the Earth.

mcqs.q: An external force moves a 3.0 kg mass at constant speed from a point where the gravitational potential is −3.2 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹ to a point where it is −1.1 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. What is the work done on the mass by the external force?
mcqs.specStatementText: the work done in moving a mass m in a gravitational field as given by W = mΔV_g
mcqs.explain: W = mΔV_g = m(V_final − V_initial) = 3.0 × (−1.1 × 10⁶ − (−3.2 × 10⁶)) = 3.0 × 2.1 × 10⁶ = +6.3 × 10⁶ J. The mass moves to a higher (less negative) potential, so positive work is done.
mcqs.working: ΔV_g = V_final − V_initial = −1.1 × 10⁶ − (−3.2 × 10⁶) = +2.1 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. W = mΔV_g = 3.0 kg × 2.1 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹ = +6.3 × 10⁶ J.
rationales: W = mΔV_g = m(V_final − V_initial) = 3.0 × (−1.1 × 10⁶ − (−3.2 × 10⁶)) = 3.0 × 2.1 × 10⁶ = +6.3 × 10⁶ J. The mass moves to a higher (less negative) potential, so positive work is done.

A student who sees the size of the potential fall from 3.2 to 1.1 thinks the potential energy decreases and gives a negative answer. −1.1 × 10⁶ is higher than −3.2 × 10⁶, so the potential energy rises and the work done on the mass is positive.
A student who treats the potential difference as the work done omits the mass. ΔV_g = 2.1 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹ is the work per kilogram; for 3.0 kg, W = mΔV_g = 6.3 × 10⁶ J.

A student who uses the potential at the starting point alone, W = mV_g = 3.0 × (−3.2 × 10⁶), gets −9.6 × 10⁶ J. mV_g at one point is the work done bringing the mass in from infinity; here the mass moves between two points, so W = mΔV_g, using the difference in potential.

mcqs.q: An 800 kg satellite is launched from rest on the surface of a non-rotating planet of mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m, and placed in a circular orbit of radius 1.00 × 10⁷ m. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Ignoring air resistance, what is the minimum energy that must be supplied to the satellite?
mcqs.specStatementText: the work done in moving a mass m in a gravitational field as given by W = mΔV_g
mcqs.explain: Energy supplied = E_total in orbit − E_p at surface = −GMm/2r − (−GMm/R) = 3.186 × 10¹⁷ × (1/6.37 × 10⁶ − 1/2.00 × 10⁷) = 5.001 × 10¹⁰ − 1.593 × 10¹⁰ = 3.41 × 10¹⁰ J.
mcqs.working: GMm = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹)(5.97 × 10²⁴)(800) = 3.186 × 10¹⁷ J m. Initial energy (rest, non-rotating planet): E = −GMm/R = −5.001 × 10¹⁰ J. Final energy in circular orbit: E = −GMm/2r = −1.593 × 10¹⁰ J. Energy supplied = −1.593 × 10¹⁰ − (−5.001 × 10¹⁰) = 3.41 × 10¹⁰ J (ΔE_p = 1.82 × 10¹⁰ J plus E_k = 1.59 × 10¹⁰ J).
rationales: A student who thinks the satellite only has to be lifted to the orbit's height calculates the gain in E_p alone, GMm(1/R − 1/r) = 1.82 × 10¹⁰ J. Left at rest there, it would fall back; it also needs E_k = GMm/2r = 1.59 × 10¹⁰ J.

A student who takes the orbital kinetic energy as GMm/r, forgetting the ½, adds 3.19 × 10¹⁰ J to the gain in E_p and gets 5.00 × 10¹⁰ J (which is the energy to escape from the surface). E_k = ½mv² = GMm/2r = 1.59 × 10¹⁰ J.
Energy supplied = E_total in orbit − E_p at surface = −GMm/2r − (−GMm/R) = 3.186 × 10¹⁷ × (1/6.37 × 10⁶ − 1/2.00 × 10⁷) = 5.001 × 10¹⁰ − 1.593 × 10¹⁰ = 3.41 × 10¹⁰ J.
A student who thinks reaching orbit is only a matter of reaching orbital speed gives the orbital kinetic energy alone. Rising from the surface to r = 1.00 × 10⁷ m also increases E_p by 1.82 × 10¹⁰ J.

mcqs.q: Equipotential surfaces are drawn around an isolated planet that is a uniform sphere, at equal intervals of gravitational potential. Which description is correct?
options: Concentric spheres, equally spaced at all distances from the planet's centre.
Concentric spheres, further apart the further they are from the planet.
Radial straight lines that point inwards towards the planet's centre.
Concentric spheres, on each of which the gravitational field strength is zero.
mcqs.specStatementText: equipotential surfaces for gravitational fields
mcqs.explain: V_g = −GM/r depends only on r, so equipotentials are spheres centred on the planet. Equal steps in V_g need larger steps in r further out, where the field is weaker, so the spacing increases with distance.
rationales: A student who transfers the uniform-field pattern picks this. In a radial field V_g changes more slowly with r further out, so equal steps of potential are further apart there.

V_g = −GM/r depends only on r, so equipotentials are spheres centred on the planet. Equal steps in V_g need larger steps in r further out, where the field is weaker, so the spacing increases with distance.
A student who confuses equipotentials with field lines picks this. Radial lines are the field lines; the equipotentials cross them at right angles, forming concentric spheres.

A student who thinks there is no field where the potential is constant picks this. On each sphere the potential does not change along the surface, but the field is perpendicular to it and equal to GM/r² there.

mcqs.q: A small mass is moved along an equipotential surface in a gravitational field. Which statement is correct?
options: There is no gravitational field on the surface, so no force acts on the mass.
Gravity does work on the mass, as its weight acts on it all the time it moves.
The field acts along the surface, in the same direction as the mass moves.
The field is perpendicular to its path, so gravity does no work on the mass.
mcqs.specStatementText: the relationship between equipotential surfaces and gravitational field lines
mcqs.explain: Field lines cross equipotential surfaces at right angles, so the gravitational force has no component along the path. With W = mΔV_g and ΔV_g = 0, no work is done by gravity.
rationales: A student who thinks constant potential means no field picks this. The field is not zero; it is perpendicular to the surface, so it does no work along it. A satellite in a circular orbit moves along an equipotential under a large gravitational force.
A student who thinks any force on a moving object does work picks this. Work needs a force component along the displacement, W = Fs cos θ; here θ = 90°, so the work done is zero.

A student who thinks field lines run along equipotentials picks this. If the field had a component along the surface, the potential would change along it, contradicting the definition of an equipotential.
Field lines cross equipotential surfaces at right angles, so the gravitational force has no component along the path. With W = mΔV_g and ΔV_g = 0, no work is done by gravity.

mcqs.q: The Moon has mass 7.35 × 10²² kg and radius 1.74 × 10⁶ m. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². What is the escape speed from a point 2.00 × 10⁶ m above the Moon's surface?
mcqs.specStatementText: the escape speed v_esc at any point in a gravitational field as given by v_esc = √(2GM/r)
rationales: A student who uses the height, 2.00 × 10⁶ m, as r gets 2.21 × 10³ m s⁻¹. r is measured from the Moon's centre: r = R + h = 3.74 × 10⁶ m.

A student who treats the escape speed as a fixed property of the Moon gives the surface value, √(2GM/R) = 2.37 × 10³ m s⁻¹. Further out less energy is needed to reach infinity, so the escape speed is lower.
A student who thinks an orbiting body has escaped gives the orbital speed, √(GM/r) = 1.14 × 10³ m s⁻¹. A body moving at this speed stays bound in orbit; escape needs √2 times as much.

mcqs.q: A satellite is in a circular orbit around a planet and has kinetic energy E_k. What is the minimum extra energy that must be given to the satellite for it to escape the gravitational influence of the planet?
options: 2E_k, the magnitude of its gravitational potential energy
3E_k, since escape speed is twice the orbital speed
E_k, which raises its total energy from −E_k to zero
No finite amount, as the field reaches to infinity
mcqs.specStatementText: the escape speed v_esc at any point in a gravitational field as given by v_esc = √(2GM/r)
mcqs.explain: In a circular orbit E_k = GMm/2r and E_p = −GMm/r = −2E_k, so the total energy is −E_k. Escape needs a total energy of at least zero, so E_k more must be supplied: its kinetic energy doubles, and its speed rises by √2.
mcqs.working: Circular orbit: E_k = GMm/2r, E_p = −GMm/r = −2E_k, E_total = −E_k. Escape requires E_total ≥ 0, so the minimum extra energy is E_k (v rises from v_orbital to √2 v_orbital = v_esc).
rationales: A student who uses the escape condition for a body starting from rest supplies the full |E_p| = 2E_k. The satellite already has kinetic energy E_k, so only E_k more is needed to bring the total to zero.
A student who takes v_esc = 2v_orbital needs four times the kinetic energy, so 3E_k extra. In fact v_esc = √(2GM/r) = √2 × v_orbital: the kinetic energy only doubles.

In a circular orbit E_k = GMm/2r and E_p = −GMm/r = −2E_k, so the total energy is −E_k. Escape needs a total energy of at least zero, so E_k more must be supplied: its kinetic energy doubles, and its speed rises by √2.

A student who pictures escape as reaching a place beyond gravity picks this. The field weakens as 1/r², so the total work to reach infinity is finite. A satellite with zero total energy slows forever but never returns.

mcqs.q: A navigation satellite orbits the Earth in a circular orbit at a height of 2.02 × 10⁷ m above the surface. The Earth has mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². What is the orbital speed of the satellite?
mcqs.specStatementText: the orbital speed v_orbital of a body orbiting a large mass as given by v_orbital = √(GM/r)
rationales: A student who uses the height, 2.02 × 10⁷ m, as r gets 4.44 × 10³ m s⁻¹. The orbit's radius is measured from the Earth's centre: r = R + h = 2.657 × 10⁷ m.

A student who uses the Earth's radius as r finds the orbital speed just above the surface, 7.91 × 10³ m s⁻¹. This satellite is over four Earth radii from the centre, where the orbital speed is much lower.

A student who thinks an orbiting satellite has escaped the Earth's gravity uses the escape speed √(2GM/r). Gravity is what holds the satellite in orbit: GMm/r² = mv²/r gives v = √(GM/r), which is √2 times smaller.

mcqs.q: A satellite is moved from one circular orbit to another circular orbit of larger radius around the same planet. How does its total energy in the new orbit compare with its total energy in the old orbit?
options: Greater, because it moves faster in the larger orbit and so has more kinetic energy.
Lower, because it moves more slowly in the larger orbit and so has less kinetic energy.
Lower, because the magnitude of its potential energy, GMm/r, is smaller in the larger orbit.
Greater, because its potential energy rises by twice as much as its kinetic energy falls.
mcqs.specStatementText: the orbital speed v_orbital of a body orbiting a large mass as given by v_orbital = √(GM/r)
mcqs.explain: Moving from r₁ to r₂ > r₁, E_k = GMm/2r falls by (GMm/2)(1/r₁ − 1/r₂) while E_p = −GMm/r rises by GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂), twice as much. The total energy −GMm/2r therefore becomes less negative: greater. The satellite ends up slower but with more energy.
rationales: A student who links more energy with more speed picks this. The larger orbit needs less centripetal force, which gravity supplies at a lower speed: v = √(GM/r) and E_k = GMm/2r both fall. The total energy is greater, but the extra energy is in E_p, not E_k.
A student who counts only kinetic energy picks this. E_k = GMm/2r does fall, but E_p = −GMm/r rises by twice as much, so the total energy −GMm/2r increases. Energy must be supplied to raise an orbit.

A student who compares magnitudes and ignores the sign picks this. GMm/r is smaller in the larger orbit, but E_p = −GMm/r, so E_p becomes less negative: it increases. It rises by twice as much as E_k falls, so the total energy −GMm/2r increases.

Moving from r₁ to r₂ > r₁, E_k = GMm/2r falls by (GMm/2)(1/r₁ − 1/r₂) while E_p = −GMm/r rises by GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂), twice as much. The total energy −GMm/2r therefore becomes less negative: greater. The satellite ends up slower but with more energy.

mcqs.q: A satellite in a low circular orbit experiences a small viscous drag force from the thin upper atmosphere. Over many orbits its path remains approximately circular. How do its orbital radius and its speed change?
options: The radius gradually decreases and the orbital speed also decreases.
The radius gradually decreases while the orbital speed gradually increases.
The radius gradually increases because the orbital speed decreases.
The radius gradually decreases while the orbital speed stays the same.
mcqs.specStatementText: the qualitative effect of a small viscous drag force due to the atmosphere on the height and speed of an orbiting body.
mcqs.explain: Drag removes energy, so the total energy −GMm/2r becomes more negative and r decreases. In each smaller orbit v = √(GM/r) is larger: gravity does more positive work as the satellite spirals in than the drag does negative work.
rationales: A student who expects any resistive force to slow an object picks this. The lost energy comes from E_p: as the satellite drops, E_p falls by twice the gain in E_k, so it speeds up while it loses height.

Drag removes energy, so the total energy −GMm/2r becomes more negative and r decreases. In each smaller orbit v = √(GM/r) is larger: gravity does more positive work as the satellite spirals in than the drag does negative work.

A student who reasons 'drag slows it, and slower orbits are larger' picks this. Start from energy: drag lowers the total energy −GMm/2r, which means a smaller r, and a smaller orbit has a higher speed.

A student who thinks the orbital speed does not depend on the orbit picks this. For a circular orbit there is only one speed at each radius, v = √(GM/r), so the smaller orbit the satellite drops into must be travelled faster.

mcqs.q: A space probe approaches an asteroid that is irregular in shape and not of uniform density. While the probe is far away, the gravitational force on it is given accurately by F = GMm/r², with r measured from the asteroid's centre of mass. Close to the asteroid's surface the same equation is no longer accurate. Which statement explains these observations?
options: No body acts as a point mass when it is close: even a sphere of uniform density can be treated as a point mass at its centre only when the distance to it is large compared with its radius, as here.

The point-mass model needs the probe's mass to be negligible compared with the asteroid's; an asteroid is so small that this condition only holds while the probe is far away, and it breaks down as the probe closes in.
Far away, the asteroid's size is negligible compared with r, so it acts as a point mass; close up, its mass is not distributed spherically, so its field is not that of a point mass at its centre.
Close to the asteroid, r should be measured from the asteroid's surface to the probe rather than from its centre of mass, because the surface is where the attraction on the probe begins.
mcqs.specStatementText: conditions under which extended bodies can be treated as point masses
mcqs.explain: Any body acts as a point mass when r is large compared with its dimensions. The exact result at every distance holds only for a sphere of uniform density (or spherical shells); an irregular, non-uniform asteroid gives a field close to its surface that differs from GM/r² about its centre of mass.
rationales: A student who thinks the point-mass model is only a far-away approximation picks this. For a sphere of uniform density the result is exact at every point outside it, however close. The failure here is due to the asteroid's irregular shape and non-uniform density, not to closeness alone.

A student who hears 'point mass' as 'small mass' picks this. The mass ratio of probe to asteroid is the same at every distance and is irrelevant to whether a body's field is that of a point mass; what matters is how the asteroid's mass is distributed in space.

Any body acts as a point mass when r is large compared with its dimensions. The exact result at every distance holds only for a sphere of uniform density (or spherical shells); an irregular, non-uniform asteroid gives a field close to its surface that differs from GM/r² about its centre of mass.

A student who takes r as the gap between the surfaces picks this. In Newton's law r is the separation of the centres of mass; changing where r is measured from does not turn an irregular body into a point mass. Every part of the asteroid attracts the probe, and close up these attractions do not add to the field of a point at the centre.

mcqs.q: Two identical stars, each of mass M, are at rest with their centres a distance r apart. A student argues that each star 'has' a gravitational potential energy of −GM²/r in the field of the other, so that the total gravitational potential energy of the two-star system is −2GM²/r. Which statement correctly assesses this claim?
options: The claim is right: potential energy belongs to a body placed in a field, and each star sits in the gravitational field of the other, so each star has −GM²/r of its own.
The claim has the sign wrong: work must be done against gravity to bring the stars together from infinity, so each star has +GM²/r and the total for the two is +2GM²/r.
The claim ignores direction: each star's potential energy is directed towards the other star, so the two values cancel and the system's total is zero.
The claim double-counts: −GM²/r is the whole work done in bringing the stars together from infinite separation, and belongs to the pair, not to either star.
mcqs.specStatementText: that the gravitational potential energy E_p of a system is the work done to assemble the system from infinite separation of the components of the system
mcqs.explain: E_p of a system is the work done to assemble it from infinite separation. Whether star A is brought up to star B or both are moved, the total work done by the external agent is −GM²/r. That single quantity is the potential energy of the pair; there is no separate E_p for each star to add.
rationales: A student who attaches potential energy to an individual body picks this. E_p is a property of the interacting pair, defined by the work done to assemble the system. Counting −GM²/r once for each star counts the same assembly work twice.

A student who thinks assembling the system needs positive work picks this. The stars attract, so the external agent holds them back and does negative work; E_p at any finite separation is negative. The doubling is also wrong, since E_p belongs to the pair.

A student who reads the minus sign as a direction picks this. Energy is a scalar; the sign of E_p records that the system has less energy than at infinite separation, and scalars cannot point in opposite directions and cancel.

E_p of a system is the work done to assemble it from infinite separation. Whether star A is brought up to star B or both are moved, the total work done by the external agent is −GM²/r. That single quantity is the potential energy of the pair; there is no separate E_p for each star to add.

mcqs.q: A graph shows the gravitational potential V_g along a radial line from the centre of a planet, plotted against the distance r from the centre. Which statement about the gravitational field strength g at a point outside the planet on this line is correct?
options: g is the gradient of the graph at that point, so the field is directed towards higher V_g, outwards.
g is fixed by the value of V_g at that point alone, and does not depend on how V_g changes with r near the point.
g is minus the gradient of the graph at that point, so the field is directed towards lower V_g.
g is zero at that point whenever the point lies on an equipotential surface, however steep the graph is there.
mcqs.specStatementText: the gravitational field strength g as the gravitational potential gradient as given by g = −ΔV_g/Δr
mcqs.explain: g = −ΔV_g/Δr: the field strength is the negative of the potential gradient. Outside a planet V_g increases (becomes less negative) with r, so the gradient is positive and g is negative, meaning the field points towards decreasing r, where the potential is lower.
rationales: A student who drops the minus sign picks this. The gradient of V_g against r is positive outside a planet, but the field points inwards, towards lower potential; g = −ΔV_g/Δr makes this explicit.

A student who reads a field from a single potential value picks this. The potential at one point can be shifted by choosing a different zero without changing the field; g depends on the rate of change of V_g with distance, the gradient of the graph.

g = −ΔV_g/Δr: the field strength is the negative of the potential gradient. Outside a planet V_g increases (becomes less negative) with r, so the gradient is positive and g is negative, meaning the field points towards decreasing r, where the potential is lower.

A student who thinks constant potential means no field picks this. Every point lies on some equipotential surface. The potential is constant along the surface but changes across it, and it is that change with r, the gradient of the graph, that gives g.

mcqs.q: The Earth has mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m, and the gravitational field strength at its surface is 9.8 N kg⁻¹. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². An equipotential surface around the Earth has gravitational potential V_g = −2.50 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹. What is the radius of this surface, measured from the centre of the Earth?
mcqs.specStatementText: equipotential surfaces for gravitational fields
mcqs.explain: An equipotential around a spherical mass is a sphere on which V_g = −GM/r has one value, so r = GM/|V_g| = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴)/(2.50 × 10⁷) = 1.59 × 10⁷ m, measured from the centre.
mcqs.working: V_g = −GM/r, so r = GM/|V_g| = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)(5.97 × 10²⁴ kg)/(2.50 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹) = 3.982 × 10¹⁴ / 2.50 × 10⁷ = 1.593 × 10⁷ m ≈ 1.59 × 10⁷ m. This is about 2.5 Earth radii from the centre, i.e. a height of 9.56 × 10⁶ m above the surface.
rationales: A student who thinks the r in V_g = −GM/r is the height above the surface computes GM/|V_g| = 1.59 × 10⁷ m, calls it a height, and adds the Earth's radius. The r in the equation is already the distance from the centre, so nothing should be added.
A student who confuses potential with field strength uses |V_g| = GM/r² and gets r = √(GM/|V_g|) = 3.99 × 10³ m, a distance far inside the Earth. Potential falls as 1/r, not 1/r²: r = GM/|V_g|.
An equipotential around a spherical mass is a sphere on which V_g = −GM/r has one value, so r = GM/|V_g| = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴)/(2.50 × 10⁷) = 1.59 × 10⁷ m, measured from the centre.

A student who takes potential as zero at the surface and equal to gh above it sets h = 2.50 × 10⁷/9.8 = 2.55 × 10⁶ m and adds the Earth's radius. Potential is zero at infinity and V_g = −GM/r; the field is far from uniform over such heights, so gh does not apply.

mcqs.q: A small mass is at a point P on an equipotential surface in the gravitational field of a planet. It is to be moved a short distance from P. In which direction should it be moved so that the gravitational force does the greatest positive work on it?
options: Perpendicular to the equipotential surface and towards the planet, so that it moves along the field line through P towards lower potential.
Perpendicular to the equipotential surface and away from the planet, so that it moves towards higher potential more quickly.
Along the equipotential surface, because the gravitational field acts along the surface rather than across it.
In any direction, because the gravitational force does the same work over the same distance whichever way the mass moves.
mcqs.specStatementText: the relationship between equipotential surfaces and gravitational field lines
mcqs.explain: Field lines cross equipotential surfaces at right angles and point towards lower potential. Work done by gravity is W = −mΔV_g, so the greatest positive work over a short distance comes from the largest fall in V_g, which is along the field line, perpendicular to the surface and towards the planet.
rationales: Field lines cross equipotential surfaces at right angles and point towards lower potential. Work done by gravity is W = −mΔV_g, so the greatest positive work over a short distance comes from the largest fall in V_g, which is along the field line, perpendicular to the surface and towards the planet.

A student who thinks the field points towards increasing potential picks this. Moving to higher V_g means ΔV_g > 0, so gravity does negative work, W = −mΔV_g < 0; positive work by gravity requires a fall in potential, which is towards the planet.
A student who thinks field lines run along equipotentials picks this. The field is perpendicular to an equipotential surface; along the surface ΔV_g = 0, so gravity does no work at all.

A student who thinks a force does work whatever the angle to the motion picks this. W = Fs cos θ: the work depends on the direction of the displacement relative to the force, and is greatest when the mass moves along the field, towards the planet.

mcqs.q: A satellite in a low circular orbit around a planet experiences a small viscous drag force from the thin upper atmosphere. Over many orbits it spirals slowly inwards, its orbit remaining approximately circular. Which statement about the energy changes is correct?
options: The kinetic energy of the satellite decreases, because the drag force acts against its motion and so does negative work on it throughout.
The gravitational potential energy of the system increases as the satellite moves inwards, because GMm/r becomes larger.
The kinetic energy of the satellite increases, because the fall in potential energy exceeds the energy transferred to the atmosphere by drag.
The total energy of the satellite–planet system is unchanged, because the loss of gravitational potential energy equals the gain in kinetic energy.
mcqs.specStatementText: the qualitative effect of a small viscous drag force due to the atmosphere on the height and speed of an orbiting body.
mcqs.explain: For a circular orbit E_k = GMm/2r and E_p = −GMm/r, so as r falls E_p drops by twice the rise in E_k. Half the lost E_p goes into E_k and half is transferred to the atmosphere by drag; the satellite therefore speeds up while it loses height.
rationales: A student who expects any resistive force to slow an object picks this. Drag does do negative work, but as the satellite spirals inwards gravity does more positive work on it than drag does negative work, so its kinetic energy rises and it moves faster in the smaller orbit.

A student who looks at the size of GMm/r and forgets the sign picks this. E_p = −GMm/r is negative and becomes more negative as r decreases, so the potential energy falls as the satellite moves inwards.

For a circular orbit E_k = GMm/2r and E_p = −GMm/r, so as r falls E_p drops by twice the rise in E_k. Half the lost E_p goes into E_k and half is transferred to the atmosphere by drag; the satellite therefore speeds up while it loses height.

A student who applies energy conservation without including the atmosphere picks this. Drag transfers energy out of the satellite–planet system, so its total energy −GMm/2r falls; E_k rises by only half of the fall in E_p, the other half going to the atmosphere.

scopeNotes.statement: For calculations involving orbital motion the orbits will be assumed to be circular.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Kepler's first and second laws are tested only qualitatively for elliptical orbits (q02: the Sun at a focus rather than the centre, the comet fastest nearest the Sun). Every orbital calculation, including the Kepler's third law calculation in q03, treats the orbits as circles of radius r; no item calculates anything for an ellipse.

scopeNotes.statement: The orbital motion of a satellite around a planet is restricted to a consideration of circular orbits.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every satellite item (q05, q13, q19, q23, q24, q25, q26, q32) states or assumes a circular orbit, so v_orbital = √(GM/r), E_k = GMm/2r and E_total = −GMm/2r apply. No item involves elliptical transfer orbits or speeds at perigee and apogee.

scopeNotes.statement: Newton’s universal law of gravitation should be extended to spherical masses of uniform density by assuming that their mass is concentrated at their centre.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Planets, moons and the Sun are always described as uniform spheres (or treated as such) and r is always measured from their centres. No item asks for the field inside a body or for the force between non-spherical bodies.

scopeNotes.statement: Newton’s universal law of gravitation should be extended to spherical masses of uniform density by assuming that their mass is concentrated at their centre.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Two conditions are tested: the one the guidance sets, that outside a uniform sphere the field is that of a point mass at its centre even for a satellite close to the surface (q06), and the general large-separation condition under which a body of any shape acts as a point mass (q27, an irregular asteroid, tested qualitatively). No item derives the result, treats the field inside a sphere, or calculates a force for a non-spherical body.

scopeNotes.statement: Determination of the resultant gravitational field strength will be restricted to points along a line joining two bodies.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The only resultant-field item (q09) is on the line joining the centres of the Earth and the Moon, where the two fields are antiparallel and simply subtract. No item adds field vectors at an angle.

scopeNotes.statement: Gravitational fields will include the radial fields around point or spherical masses and the (assumed) uniform field close to the surface of massive celestial bodies and planetary bodies.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Items use only the radial field of a point or spherical mass (q05, q08, q09, q16, q22, q24) and the assumed uniform field close to a planet's surface (q11). No other field geometry is used.

scopeNotes.statement: Sketching and interpretation of gravitational field lines is required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Because no diagram can be shown, field-line patterns are described in words and the student chooses the correct description (q10) or interprets a described pattern (q11); the reasoning a sketch supports (direction, spacing, uniform versus radial) is what is tested.

scopeNotes.statement: Gravitational potential is defined as being zero at infinity.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: V_g = 0 and E_p = 0 at infinity throughout, so every potential and potential energy is negative. The belief that V_g or E_p is zero at a planet's surface is treated as a misconception (m36), not as an alternative convention.

scopeNotes.statement: An ability to map fields using potential is required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Mapping the field using potential is tested by finding g from two equipotential values and their separation (q17), by the spacing of equipotential surfaces (q20) and by the perpendicular relationship between field lines and equipotentials (q21).

scopeNotes.statement: Problems may include, but are not limited to, determining the: • speed to maintain orbit • changes in energy when a satellite changes orbit • energetics of a satellite going into orbit around a non-rotating planet starting from rest on its surface • energy conditions for an orbiting satellite to escape the gravitational influence of a planet.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: All four problem types in the guidance appear: speed to maintain orbit (q24), energy change on changing orbit (q13, q25), energetics of going into orbit from rest on a non-rotating planet (q19), and the energy condition for an orbiting satellite to escape (q23). Planetary rotation is never used to reduce the launch energy.
